questions.question: 1. If there are 10 edges in a graph, in the worst case how many edges can DFS examine?

explanations.a: Incorrect. DFS may need to examine edges in order to explore the graph.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A graph containing multiple edges may require DFS to examine more than one edge.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS is not limited to examining only half of the edges in the graph.
explanations.d: Correct. In an appropriate graph representation, DFS may need to examine all 10 edges during traversal.

questions.question: 2. Which one of the following statements correctly compares DFS and BFS?

answers.a: DFS uses a queue, while BFS uses a stack.
answers.b: In DFS, all neighbors are always traversed before any deeper vertex is explored.
answers.c: DFS is a vertex-based algorithm while BFS is an edge-based algorithm.
answers.d: BFS can find a shortest path in an unweighted graph, whereas DFS does not guarantee a shortest path.

explanations.a: Incorrect. The standard implementations use different traversal structures from those stated here.
explanations.b: Incorrect. DFS can move deeper along a path before all neighboring vertices of the current vertex have been explored.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Both DFS and BFS systematically process vertices and examine edges.
explanations.d: Correct. BFS explores an unweighted graph level by level and can therefore find a shortest path in terms of the number of edges, while DFS does not provide that guarantee.

questions.question: 3. What is the primary goal of DFS when it is started from a particular source vertex?

answers.a: To explore reachable vertices by going as deep as possible before backtracking.
answers.b: To visit only the immediate neighbors of the source.
answers.d: To remove all edges from the graph.

explanations.a: Correct. DFS explores reachable vertices by following a path deeply and backtracking when necessary.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Limiting the traversal to immediate neighbors would not explore the graph deeply.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Sorting vertex labels is not the purpose of DFS.
explanations.d: Incorrect. DFS traverses the graph without removing its edges.

questions.question: 4. What happens when DFS reaches a vertex whose adjacent vertices have already been visited?

answers.b: DFS backtracks to an earlier vertex to continue exploring another available path.
answers.d: DFS changes the graph from directed to undirected.

explanations.a: Incorrect. DFS does not create new vertices during traversal.
explanations.b: Correct. When there are no unvisited adjacent vertices to continue from the current vertex, DFS backtracks to an earlier vertex.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Reaching a fully explored vertex does not cause DFS to delete it.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Traversal does not change whether the graph is directed or undirected.

questions.question: 5. Which data structure is commonly used to implement iterative DFS?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A queue is associated with the usual breadth-first traversal strategy.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A heap is not the standard data structure used to control the order of iterative DFS.
explanations.c: Correct. Iterative DFS commonly uses a stack to keep track of vertices that still need to be explored.
explanations.d: Incorrect. DFS does not require vertices to be processed according to priority.

questions.question: 6. Why can recursion be used to implement DFS?

answers.b: Recursion removes the need to mark vertices as visited.
answers.c: Recursion converts the graph into a tree.
answers.d: The function call stack naturally stores the pending vertices and supports backtracking.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Recursion does not automatically sort vertices or edges.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A visited mechanism may still be required to prevent repeated processing of vertices.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Using recursion does not change the original graph structure.
explanations.d: Correct. Recursive function calls use the call stack, which naturally preserves the traversal state needed to return to earlier vertices.

questions.question: 7. For an adjacency-list representation, why is the DFS complexity $O(V + E)$ rather than $O(V^2)$ in general?

answers.a: DFS ignores edges that are not part of the DFS tree.
answers.b: DFS visits only half of the vertices.
answers.c: The adjacency list allows DFS to examine the actual edges associated with each visited vertex instead of checking every possible vertex pair.
answers.d: DFS never examines an edge more than once in either direction.

explanations.a: Incorrect. DFS may examine edges that do not become tree edges, including edges leading to already visited vertices.
explanations.b: Incorrect. DFS can visit every vertex that is reachable from its starting point.
explanations.c: Correct. An adjacency list stores the actual neighbors of each vertex, so DFS processes the vertices and the listed edges, giving $O(V + E)$ time.
explanations.d: Incorrect. In an undirected graph, an edge can appear in the adjacency lists of both of its endpoints and may therefore be examined from both sides.

questions.question: 8. Which property of DFS makes it useful for detecting cycles in a graph?

answers.a: DFS records traversal relationships and can identify an edge leading to a vertex that is already active in the current traversal path.
answers.b: DFS always visits every vertex exactly twice.
answers.c: DFS removes every edge after examining it.
answers.d: DFS requires the graph to contain no cycles before it starts.

explanations.a: Correct. DFS maintains traversal information that can be used to identify edges connecting a vertex to an ancestor or an active vertex, which is important for cycle detection.
explanations.b: Incorrect. DFS does not require every vertex to be visited exactly twice.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS examines edges but does not remove them from the graph.
explanations.d: Incorrect. DFS can be used precisely to investigate whether cycles are present.

questions.question: 9. A DFS is started from vertex $A$ in a connected graph. If the graph contains 8 vertices, how many vertices will be visited by the DFS?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A connected graph contains paths from the starting vertex to all other vertices.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A connected graph does not restrict DFS to only half of its vertices.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The starting vertex and the other reachable vertices together make the complete set of vertices in the connected graph.
explanations.d: Correct. Because the graph is connected, every one of its 8 vertices is reachable from $A$, so DFS visits all 8 vertices.
